column1: What is the fundamental wire-format invariant shared by HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 messages?
column2: Each message consists of a start-line, zero or more CRLF-delimited header fields, a mandatory blank line ending the header section, and an optional body—this grammar is constant; only framing/transport changes.

column1: Which RFC superseded RFC 7231 as the authoritative definition of HTTP semantics, and in what year?
Define 'safe' and 'idempotent' as formal HTTP method properties per RFC 9110.
column2: Safe: the method has no observable side effects on server state (e.g., GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE). Idempotent: identical repeated requests produce the same server-side effect as a single request. All safe methods are idempotent, but not all idempotent methods are safe (e.g., PUT, DELETE).

column1: Why is POST neither safe nor idempotent, while PUT is idempotent but not safe?
column2: POST creates a new side effect on each call (e.g., submitting an order twice creates two orders), so repetition changes state further. PUT to a fixed resource with the same payload results in the same end state regardless of repetition, but the first call still changes state, so it's not safe.

column1: What is the key architectural distinction between HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 transport layers?
column2: HTTP/2 multiplexes binary frames over a single TLS stream atop TCP, eliminating application-layer head-of-line blocking but still subject to TCP-level HOL blocking. HTTP/3 replaces TCP with QUIC (UDP-based, TLS 1.3 baked into handshake), eliminating transport-layer HOL blocking as well.

column1: How do authentication and authorization differ as orthogonal security invariants?
column2: Authentication proves identity ('who are you?') via cryptographic proof, secrets, or signed assertions. Authorization enforces policy on an already-authenticated identity ('what can you do?') via access control rules. They are distinct layers that should not be conflated.

column1: Why must HTTP APIs serialize security context into every request?
column2: Because HTTP is stateless with no inherent session continuity across request-response cycles, each request must independently carry proof of identity and permission—via bearer tokens, session identifiers, or request signatures.

column1: In Postman's credential inheritance model, what principle governs how authentication configs cascade?
column2: A hierarchical inheritance model following least privilege: auth configs cascade from global workspace settings through environment overrides down to individual requests, with credentials scoped as narrowly as possible unless explicitly propagated.

column1: What is the strict temporal execution sequence in Postman's request lifecycle involving scripts?
column2: Pre-request script executes (can set variables/compute signatures) → HTTP request is constructed and dispatched → server responds → test script executes against the complete, immutable response (status, headers, body).

column1: What assertion library and JS runtime does Postman use for test scripts, and what is the effect of a failed pm.test()?
column2: Postman uses the Chai assertion library on a V8-based JavaScript runtime. A failed test does not halt execution—all results accumulate into a suite-level report—but it signals a broken contract that can fail CI/CD pipelines.

column1: What is the current version of the Postman Collection Format specification, and what does a Collection formally represent?
column2: Version 2.1. A Collection is a JSON document encoding directed acyclic graphs of request sequences along with pre-request logic, assertion contracts, and dynamic variable bindings—a versioned state machine, not just a request container.

column1: What is the 'monotonic refinement' invariant governing Postman's collection inheritance hierarchy?
column2: Child nodes (folders/requests) can specialize or override parent configuration (auth, headers, scripts) but cannot erase or invalidate parent contracts; effective config is built by merging dictionaries from root to leaf, with child values taking precedence.
